newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia goes to polls, Moslems reject outcome.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia goes to polls, Moslems reject outcome.

text.p: Bosnia voted on Saturday in post-war elections that international organisers said had gone smoothly, but the main Moslem party declared it would reject in advance the results from Serb territory.

The elections, the first since a bloody 43-month ethnic war ended last November, took place under the watchful gaze of 50,000 heavily-armed NATO-led peace troops deployed to ensure those displaced by the fighting could cross ethnic borders and return to their homes to vote.
Although organisers reported the number of refugees crossing internal borders was considerably less than expected, they expressed relief that there had been no major incidents.

Incomplete voting lists caused chaos in some areas and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which set up the elections, said voting, for a collective presidency and parliament and for assemblies in a Moslem-Croat and a Serb region, would be extended for three hours in some areas and possibly into Sunday.

International High Commissioner for Bosnia Karl Bildt said initial reports indicated the elections had gone "extremely smoothly", saying the manner in which they were conducted bore "great testimony to the strength of the commitment to peace and to the peace process itself".

But only minutes later President Alija Izetbegovic's Party of Democratic Action (SDA) charged in a letter to the U.N. Security Council that there had been serious irregularities and a lack of conditions for free and fair voting in the Bosnian Serb entity.

"These irregularities and the lack of the necessary conditions for free and fair elections have decisively flawed the vote. For the above reasons the SDA deems the results of the elections in the Serb entity to be legally invalid."
Kris Janowski, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told reporters he had received two reports of Moslems being prevented from voting in Serb-controlled territory.
He said some 600 people living in Gorazde, but voting just outside the Bosnian government town, returned to their homes after waiting hours for the Serbs to open the polling station.
He said another 12 Moslems coming from the Bosnian federation town of Travnik were prevented from voting near Serb-controlled Banja Luka after Serb authorities turned their vehicle back.
The elections were designed to give Bosnia democratic inter-ethnic institutions and re-knit ties between its Moslem, Serb and Croat communities after 43 months of war.

Although the likeliest outcome was a victory for the three main nationalist parties which led the country into conflict, international mediators were encouraged by a pledge of future cooperation from Bosnian Serb hardliners.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic told U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke her separatist Serb Democratic Party (SDS) would not boycott the new collective presidency where it will have a seat along with Moslem and Croat representatives.
Earlier on Saturday Holbrooke, the architect of the Dayton accords, had warned any side rejecting Dayton's terms that they would not receive outside aid.

"We also have some leverage left -- economic aid through the IMF and international organisations will not go to parts of the country that don't cooperate with the Dayton agreement," he told a news conference in Tuzla, northern Bosnia.
Plavsic took over from Radovan Karadzic, who was forced to step down and was barred from running for office as an indicted war criminal.
Karadzic cast his vote on Saturday, according to a U.N. spokesman, as he was entitled to do, though NATO had warned they would arrest him if they found him voting.

Almost three million electors were eligible to vote for the collective Bosnian national presidency and parliament, a president and national assembly for the Serb republic and an assembly and cantonal administrations for the federation.
Many of the Moslems who decided to vote in the Serb republic were lured by the opportunity to see homes from which they were ethnically cleansed when the war began in 1992.
There was scant political point in their going back since municipal elections which should also have been held on Saturday were postponed until November.
Only a handful of Moslems went back to vote in the area of Srebrenica where several thousand unarmed Moslem prisoners were massacred by the Bosnian Serb army after its capture last year.

One group of 21 who did make the journey and voted in the hardline nationalist town of Bratunac near Srebrenica said they were treated politely by the Serbs who included former neighbours who had helped drive them out.
